extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media-law observers, and general readers interested in libel/defamation and journalistic standards
extracted.subtask_short: libel risk analysis for news reports
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how U.S. libel law and journalistic practice apply to a high-profile magazine exposé, identifying legal defenses, plaintiff requirements, and reporting failures that affect libel liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as an absolute defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is an absolute defense to libel; if the allegedly defamatory factual assertions are true, the publisher can avoid liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone has retracted the story and acknowledges the assault did not occur, so it will not be using truth as a defense in these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion defense (non-actionable when truly opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegedly defamatory statements that are matters of opinion (rather than factual assertions) can be protected as non-actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Rolling Stone story was built on the factual assertion that a gang rape had occurred, the opinion defense likely won't help in the fraternity cases, though it may arise in the UVA administrator's suit where some claims are framed as opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Of and concerning" / identification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A defamatory statement must be shown to be 'about' or 'of and concerning' the plaintiff; plaintiffs must show the statement reasonably refers to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that no actual members of the fraternity were named and that many details were vague; courts may find the article's details 'too vague and remote' to be about particular plaintiffs. This element can defeat a libel claim if the connection to the plaintiff is not shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named individuals vs institution — pleading 'of and concerning' the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article focuses on individuals rather than the institution, a plaintiff organization must show the article stated or implied the institution itself approved or tolerated the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phi Kappa Psi will likely have to argue that the article implied the rape took place 'with the express or implied consent and approval of the fraternity' to establish the article was about the fraternity as an institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence standard for private figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Private figures alleging libel generally must show negligence on the part of the publisher (a lower standard than for public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fraternity argues it should be considered a private figure; if the judge agrees, they need only prove negligence (e.g., failures in reporting and fact-checking) rather than actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual malice / reckless disregard (New York Times v. Sullivan standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures must show 'actual malice': publishing while knowing something was false or publishing with reckless disregard for whether it was true or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This higher standard protects speech on matters of public import. The plaintiff must show the publisher actually entertained doubts about the truth of the story; discovery into editorial doubts and communications can be critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reckless-disregard requirement when private figures seek punitive damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Although actual malice is generally associated with public-figure suits, the recklessness standard can also apply when private figures seek punitive damages in addition to compensatory damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that the reckless-disregard standard may therefore become relevant even if the plaintiff is a private figure, if punitive damages are sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation per se (Virginia law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain allegations are 'defamatory per se' and plaintiffs need not prove actual harm (e.g., allegations of serious crimes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Virginia law, accusing a subject of a serious crime (like a violent sexual assault) would typically be defamation per se, easing the plaintiffs' burden on proving damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of editorial doubts and internal communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will look for evidence in emails and editorial materials that editors or reporters expressed doubts about the story's truth to establish recklessness or actual malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs are likely to 'comb through the magazine's email and editing materials' for statements showing editors had reservations. The Columbia Journalism School report and internal records are potential sources of such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic practices: reporting, editing, editorial supervision, fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional journalistic practices include thorough reporting, rigorous editing, strong editorial supervision, and careful fact-checking; setting aside these practices can indicate negligence or reckless disregard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Columbia Journalism School called the story 'a story of journalistic failure that was avoidable,' emphasizing that the failure 'encompassed reporting, editing, editorial supervision and fact-checking.' Courts may evaluate whether essential practices were 'set aside or rationalized as unnecessary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration and interviewing relevant witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should corroborate sources and interview witnesses (friends, alleged perpetrators, institution representatives) when making factual accusations; failure to do so can support a negligence/recklessness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone largely took 'Jackie's' word, did not speak to her friends, did not properly question the fraternity about specific charges, failed to identify alleged assailants, and did not interview individual fraternity members—failures that the article highlights as central to the magazine's liability exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to interview a key witness can imply deliberate ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication's deliberate decision not to interview a key witness may be characterized by courts as a deliberate decision not to acquire knowledge of facts, supporting a finding of reckless disregard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has found that not interviewing a key witness could be 'the product of a deliberate decision not to acquire knowledge of facts,' a point the article uses to explain potential evidence of recklessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication-based defamation (suggesting the institution tolerates wrongdoing or is dangerous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that imply an institution tolerates or regularly facilitates misconduct, or that a place is dangerous, can be defamatory even without explicit accusations directed at named individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volokh's 'bar' analogy is used: implying 'this bar, people routinely get raped in this bar' may be libelous of the bar. The article cites passages implying that assaults were part of fraternity activity or frequent occurrences—claims that can ground a defamation claim against the fraternity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-figure status of organizational plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an organization is treated as a public figure affects the standard of liability; courts often treat small or modest-sized businesses (and by analogy small organizations) as private figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volokh notes 'small- and modest-sized businesses are treated as private figures, despite their role in the community; the same would apply to a fraternity,' which informs strategy on pleading standards and required proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing of claims as factual versus opinion in litigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: How a publication frames its central claims (as factual assertions vs. policy or opinion claims) affects the availability of defenses and the plaintiffs' burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone may argue broader critiques of UVA's handling of sexual assault are opinion (protected), while plaintiffs will stress the story made factual allegations (unprotected). Determinations about which statements are factual versus opinion will shape outcomes.
